newsitem.title: CHINA: Asia grain traders shrug off China weather reports.
newsitem.headline: Asia grain traders shrug off China weather reports.

text.p: Grain traders on Monday shrugged off reports that Chinese production could be hit by drought this year, some saying the wheat harvest could even rise.
Grain traders polled by Reuters said they saw no indication of weather problems in China's major grain growing regions.

It was still too early in the season to panic, a U.S. trader said. Corn had only recently been planted, soybean planting was still under way and it would be another month before wheat and rapseseed yields become more clear, traders said.
"It's still only May," he said. "It's stuff that we've got to watch, and I don't think there's anything we should rush out and panic over yet."

China's official media has carried a number of reports in recent weeks that the weather is threatening crops in some major growing regions, including the northeast where most corn and soybeans are produced.
Some Asian traders said reports of weather problems often appeared in the Chinese press ahead of harvest and were perceived to be more a "just in case" measure than reporting of fact.
"Just looking at history, sometimes when the flood reports would come out you'd think that half of China was under water and you can't believe what they say," a Singapore source said.
"And anyway, it could all change tomorrow," he said.

China reaped a bumper harvest in 1996 of 490 million tonnes -- surpassing the previous record of 466 million tonnes in the previous year -- despite a five-month drought in north-central China and flooding in the southern rice-growing regions.
"As far as we know, everything is in pretty decent shape," another trader said. "The weather in the northeast has been reasonably good."
While no breakdown by grain has been officially released, wheat usually accounts for about 20 percent of the total crop.
Traders estimated 1996 wheat output at 110 million tonnes.

China's recent inactivity on the world wheat market indicated there was little expectation at the upper echelons of China's agriculture hierarchy of problems with the harvest, a source in Singapore said.
"That's a solid indication there is no problem," he said.
"We're looking at (a wheat harvest of) one to two million tonnes higher than last year, 111-112 million," he said.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture earlier this year revised down its estimates of China's wheat imports because of increased production and stocks.
China's 1997/98 wheat import estimate was cut to six million tonnes from 9.4 million, and 1996/97 imports to four million tonnes from seven million.
Some sources pointed to the recent exit of China from the corn market, after selling up to three million tonnes since the start of 1997.
China's major food selling arm COFCO had not been making any aggressive offers, a U.S. trader in Hong Kong said, and this could mean authorities were getting cautious about supply.
Another Singapore source said, however, there was little current demand in Southeast Asia for corn and U.S. and South American corn values were becoming more competitive.
He noted China had been sending substantial quantities of corn from the north to large consuming areas in the south.
By April 20, 6.25 million tonnes of grain and been shipped from the northeast to the south, the People's Daily Overseas Edition said last Thursday.
